title: SIMULATED PANEL — From AI ideas to laboratory tests
description: Ten fictional experts explore how to select AI-generated hypotheses. Authored synthetic responses across three rounds, including changes of mind and persistent disagreement. This demonstration contains no real expert opinions or empirical findings.
question: How should a research team decide which AI-generated hypotheses deserve a laboratory experiment?
claims: Every AI-generated hypothesis should receive an independent expert review before a laboratory experiment begins.
At least 20% of an exploratory research budget should be reserved for hypotheses with low initial expert confidence.
A hypothesis should be prioritised only when two independent evidence sources support it.

experts.name: Maya Foster
experts.opening: I want ideas that survive contact with an assay. A plausible mechanism is useful, but a small discriminating experiment is often more informative than another literature review.

comments: An independent experimentalist can catch an impossible assay before resources are committed.
A fixed allocation could consume scarce bench capacity with ideas that have no workable test.
Two sources reduce the risk of following an attractive story built on one unreliable result.
The automation engineer makes a good distinction between review of a new hypothesis and approval of every instrument action. I support the former.
The portfolio argument makes me less opposed, but I would reserve experimental capacity by test cost and learning value rather than a fixed fraction.
The discovery scientist persuaded me that this rule excludes genuinely new mechanisms. I would permit one strong source followed by an informative pilot.

experts.name: Daniel Cho
experts.opening: I would rank proposed experiments by what they can distinguish, record every attempted test, and compare the AI workflow with a credible baseline. Confidence should be calibrated, not merely high.

comments: An independent reviewer can challenge the proposed comparison and decision rule.
Twenty percent is not justified by a cost or information model.
Two apparently separate sources may share the same selection bias.
I retain support, provided review records a testable objection rather than a ceremonial signature.
For an explicitly exploratory portfolio, I now favour a protected minimum against the selection pressure described by the junior researcher. The fraction should be revisited using outcomes.
The data steward reinforces my concern: independence must be established, and a count of sources cannot replace their quality.

experts.name: Amara Okoye
experts.opening: Before ranking an idea, check provenance, permitted use, and whether the variables mean what the hypothesis assumes. Two datasets can reproduce the same error.

comments: Review should include the authority to use the supporting data.
Low confidence may reflect poor data quality rather than useful novelty.
Independent sources can reveal inconsistent coding or a local dataset artefact.
I retain agreement because an independent check can uncover provenance gaps that the generating system missed.
I remain undecided: the programme needs a definition that separates novelty from unresolved data defects.
The statistician showed why a two-source rule is too easy to satisfy superficially. I want an independence assessment, but I am unsure that two sources must always exist.

experts.name: Leo Martins
experts.opening: A laboratory can learn rapidly through cheap, reversible pilots. Separate the decision to test a new biological idea from the many routine machine actions inside an approved protocol.

comments: Review for every idea may become the main bottleneck for inexpensive automated pilots.
An automation platform should have room to test unexpected ideas instead of only confirming familiar ones.
A strict evidence threshold defeats the purpose of a rapid exploratory screen.
The experimentalist clarified that a short review can approve the hypothesis and protocol together, without approving each machine action. On that interpretation I now agree.
I retain support for a protected exploration budget, with a clear total resource ceiling.
I still oppose making two sources a universal prerequisite; a controlled pilot can create the second source.

experts.name: Sofia Lind
experts.opening: The unit of value is a finding someone else can challenge and repeat. Preserve failed tests, code, assay conditions and the reason each candidate was selected.

comments: An independent reviewer can detect omissions in the proposed controls and measurement plan.
A numerical novelty quota could encourage teams to relabel weak ideas as exploration.
Independent corroboration is a useful defence against local technical errors.
I still support review, but the automation argument persuades me that it should be proportionate and concise.
I am now undecided: a reserved budget could counter cherry-picking if all outcomes and selection decisions are recorded.
I retain agreement for prioritisation, while recognising that an exploratory pilot is different from prioritising a full programme.

experts.name: Noah Bennett
experts.opening: Research is a portfolio of uncertain options. I want a visible budget for exploration, explicit stopping rules, and a record of what was displaced when an idea was funded.

comments: Independent review should state the most consequential failure mode and a stop condition.
A minimum prevents short-term delivery pressure from consuming the entire portfolio.
A novel hypothesis may have only one line of support but substantial option value.
I retain agreement and would measure review delay as well as the faults it catches.
I retain support after hearing the early-career perspective; the minimum is a governance choice to protect exploration, not an estimate of optimal return.
I remain opposed to a universal gate. Independent review and a bounded pilot can be preferable to waiting for corroboration.

experts.name: Priya Shah
experts.opening: A credible process must make room for unconventional ideas from people without an established reputation. Reviewers should evaluate the proposed test, not the status of its proposer.

comments: Mandatory review can let senior gatekeepers block unfamiliar approaches.
A protected budget makes exploration a real opportunity rather than a rhetorical promise.
Requiring existing corroboration systematically favours established fields and well-funded topics.
I am less opposed after the governance proposal for written reasons and an appeal route, but those protections are not in the claim. I cannot fully endorse it.
I retain agreement, with a transparent selection process so the protected budget is accessible beyond senior investigators.
I still disagree because the rule excludes precisely the underexplored questions this process should help surface.

experts.name: Elias Morgan
experts.opening: The process needs attributable decisions and a way to challenge rejection. Independence is a relationship between people and incentives, not simply a second name on a form.

comments: Independent review can distribute responsibility if conflicts of interest are disclosed.
An explicit reserve makes the trade-off between exploration and delivery open to scrutiny.
The rule may help accountability, but the meaning of independent evidence is unclear.
I retain agreement, with written reasons and a route to contest rejection to address the junior researcher’s concern.
I still agree for an exploratory programme, provided spending and outcomes are reported consistently.
The panel made the exclusion cost concrete. I now prefer a documented justification for limited evidence over a universal two-source gate.

experts.name: Clara Weiss
experts.opening: The interesting hypotheses often lack a second established source. I would favour experiments that cheaply overturn a mechanism over plans that accumulate confirmatory citations.

comments: Review might improve experimental design or merely enforce existing assumptions; its form matters.
A protected exploratory allocation is essential if the system is to discover rather than imitate.
Genuinely new mechanisms often have only one initial clue.
I now agree after the panel distinguished concise design review from a requirement for prior consensus. A reviewer can improve the falsification test without endorsing the mechanism.
I retain agreement but favour a plain minimum rather than treating twenty percent as scientifically optimal.
I remain opposed. The experimentalist’s small discriminating pilot is a better response to scarce evidence.

experts.name: Oliver Grant
experts.opening: The relevant comparison is the expected learning per unit of constrained resource. Fixed quotas and extra review can both be sensible, but their opportunity costs should be visible.

comments: A universal review requirement may cost more than some reversible experiments.
A fixed minimum ignores variation in test costs and portfolio maturity.
Corroboration can reduce expenditure on fragile signals.
I retain disagreement. Even concise independent review has a cost, and the claim contains no exception for very cheap tests.
I retain disagreement; protecting exploration is desirable, but a universal twenty-percent floor does not follow from that objective.
I retain qualified agreement for prioritising substantial laboratory resources. Small exploratory pilots should have a different decision category.
